display_text: Menstrual cycle tracking as a monitoring variable. Track alongside training load — symptoms, cycle day, and subjective performance. Individual patterns are far more useful than population generalizations. / On phase-based training periodization, be sceptical. A systematic review of menstrual cycle effects on elite athlete performance found that of 662 papers reviewed and 218 assessed for eligibility, only seven precisely investigated a performance parameter across at least one cycle phase in elite athletes — and concluded that while various parameters are affected, the parameters themselves and the magnitude and direction of effects are inconclusive (Meignié et al., 2021). A more recent review in the strength and conditioning literature stated the position plainly: research does not currently support the idea that periodizing strength or endurance training according to the menstrual cycle confers additional benefit over traditional approaches. / Practical position: track the cycle, learn *your own* patterns, adjust individually based on your data, and do not adopt a rigid phase-based template on the basis of social media claims. If you consistently perform worse or feel worse in a particular phase, that is real for you and worth accommodating.

display_text: Menstrual cycle tracking as a monitoring variable. Track alongside training load — symptoms, cycle day, and subjective performance. Individual patterns are far more useful than population generalizations. / On phase-based training periodization, be sceptical. A systematic review of menstrual cycle effects on elite athlete performance found that of 662 papers reviewed and 218 assessed for eligibility, only seven precisely investigated a performance parameter across at least one cycle phase in elite athletes — and concluded that while various parameters are affected, the parameters themselves and the magnitude and direction of effects are inconclusive (Meignié et al., 2021). A more recent review in the strength and conditioning literature stated the position plainly: research does not currently support the idea that periodizing strength or endurance training according to the menstrual cycle confers additional benefit over traditional approaches. / Practical position: track the cycle, learn *your own* patterns, adjust individually based on your data, and do not adopt a rigid phase-based template on the basis of social media claims. If you consistently perform worse or feel worse in a particular phase, that is real for you and worth accommodating.

(2007), pooling 27 studies of competitive athletes, found: / - Overall taper effect on performance: 0.59 (moderate) / - Optimal strategy: a 2-week taper in which training volume is reduced exponentially by 41–60% (effect 0.72), with no modification of training intensity (effect 0.33 for maintained intensity) or frequency (0.35 for maintained frequency) / - Reducing intensity does not improve performance / A more recent systematic review and meta-analysis in endurance athletes (Chen et al., 2023) confirmed the pattern: reducing volume 41–60% while maintaining intensity and frequency, over ≤7 days, 8–14 days, or 15–21 days, in either a progressive or step pattern, significantly improved time-trial performance — and a taper preceded by a pre-taper overload block produced larger gains than a conventional taper. / Note also, relevant to strength retention: reduced-volume training during a taper clearly beats stopping altogether. Complete cessation for several weeks costs roughly twice the strength and velocity that maintained lower-volume training does. / Bosquet et al. display_text: Meta-analytic work on tapering is unusually clear and unusually actionable. Bosquet et al. (2007), pooling 27 studies of competitive athletes, found: / - Overall taper effect on performance: 0.59 (moderate) / - Optimal strategy: a 2-week taper in which training volume is reduced exponentially by 41–60% (effect 0.72), with no modification of training intensity (effect 0.33 for maintained intensity) or frequency (0.35 for maintained frequency) / - Reducing intensity does not improve performance / A more recent systematic review and meta-analysis in endurance athletes (Chen et al., 2023) confirmed the pattern: reducing volume 41–60% while maintaining intensity and frequency, over ≤7 days, 8–14 days, or 15–21 days, in either a progressive or step pattern, significantly improved time-trial performance — and a taper preceded by a pre-taper overload block produced larger gains than a conventional taper. / Note also, relevant to strength retention: reduced-volume training during a taper clearly beats stopping altogether. Complete cessation for several weeks costs roughly twice the strength and velocity that maintained lower-volume training does. / Bosquet et al. (2007), meta-analysis of 27 studies of competitive athletes: - Overall taper effect on performance: 0.59 - Optimal: 2-week taper, volume reduced exponentially by 41–60% (effect 0.72), intensity unchanged (0.33 for maintained), frequency unchanged (0.35 for maintained) - Reducing intensity does not improve performance

display_text: Diaphragmatic breathing — daily, 5–10 min - Sit or lie with one hand on the belly, one on the chest. The belly hand moves; the chest hand does not - Progress to a 4-2-6 pattern: inhale 4 s, hold 2 s, exhale 6 s. The extended exhale is the parasympathetic driver - Then practise it in the 60-second interval between rounds, on the bag and in sparring, until it is automatic. This is the transfer step everyone omits - Morning and pre-sleep / Progressive muscular relaxation — 2×/week, 15–20 min - Full-body protocol: tense each muscle group 5 s, release 15 s, moving systematically - Then build an abbreviated version usable in the ring: jaw, shoulders, hands — three checkpoints you can run in two seconds between exchanges / Cue words for relaxation - Anchor 2–3 words during training (“loose,” “breathe,” “long,” “soft hands”) and deploy them in competition - The anchoring matters: the word must be paired with the physical state hundreds of times in training before it will produce the state under pressure / HRV biofeedback — 3–5×/week, 10–15 min, if available - Resonance-frequency breathing training with a validated app and a chest strap - The evidence is moderate and the practice is harmless; worth doing if you will do it consistently

display_text: On the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR): you will encounter this metric. It divides the last 7 days’ load by a rolling ~28-day average, with the idea that a ratio around 0.8–1.3 is a “sweet spot” and spikes above ~1.5 elevate injury risk. It is intuitive and widely used, and it has been substantively criticized on methodological grounds — the mathematical coupling of numerator and denominator, arbitrary time windows, and questions about whether it predicts anything beyond simple weekly load change. Use it as a rough flag if you like it, not as a decision rule. Week-on-week load change plus monotony plus your subjective readiness data will serve you at least as well.

display_text: Two weeks out: finalize the gameplan; begin tactical imagery of it. Reduce novelty in all life domains — this is not the week to start a new job, move house, or change your diet. / Fight week: fixed daily routine, minimal decisions, imagery of plans A, B and C. Avoid opponent-related social media and outcome-focused conversation. / Day before: weigh-in routine rehearsed and executed as practised. Light technical work. Early night. No last-minute technical changes — nothing new in the final 72 hours. / Fight day: 1. Fixed wake time, fixed meals, fixed timing — all rehearsed in camp so nothing is novel 2. Low-stimulation period: music or silence per personal preference, established months in advance, not decided on the day 3. Structured warm-up, identical every time. The ritual is doing psychological work as much as physical 4. Pre-performance routine in the final 5 minutes: breathing pattern → 3 cue words → 10-second imagery of the first exchange → physical activation 5. In the ring, between rounds: breathe first (4-2-6), then listen. Boxers who talk in the corner do not hear the corner / Post-bout: immediate physical recovery and medical check. No tactical analysis for 24–48 hours. Then structured video review against the Part 2 §4 KPIs, one technical fix, one tactical fix, one documented lesson.

display_text: The Amsterdam 2023 international consensus statement (Patricios et al., 2023, *BJSM* — the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport) provides the current framework, including an updated staged return-to-play protocol and updated assessment tools (SCAT6, Child SCAT6, SCOAT6, CRT6). The consensus organizes clinical management around a framework of “R”s — Recognize, Reduce, Remove, Re-evaluate, (Relative) Rest, Rehabilitate, Refer, Recover, Return-to-Learn/Return-to-Sport, Reconsider, Refine, and Retire — the last two being additions in the Amsterdam statement. / The staged progression, adapted for boxing: / | Stage | Activity | Boxing content | Criteria to progress | / | 1 | Symptom-limited activity | Daily activities that do not exacerbate symptoms; light walking | Tolerated without symptom exacerbation | / | 2 | Light aerobic exercise | Walking, stationary bike at low intensity | 24 h symptom-free at this level | / | 3 | Sport-specific exercise, no head impact | Shadow boxing, footwork, light bag work, running | 24 h symptom-free | / | 4 | Non-contact training drills | Full technical training, pads, bag work at normal intensity, conditioning, strength training | 24 h symptom-free | / | 5 | Full contact practice — requires medical clearance | Return to sparring, beginning at Stage 3–4 of the sparring continuum, not at the level you left | Medical clearance obtained; no symptoms | / | 6 | Return to competition | Normal competitive activity | All above cleared | / Rules: - Each stage requires at least 24 hours symptom-free before progressing - Any symptom recurrence returns the athlete to the previous stage - Stage 5 requires medical clearance, without exception - On return to sparring, drop back two stages of the sparring continuum and rebuild. Returning directly to hard sparring after a concussion is how second injuries happen - Most jurisdictions impose mandatory suspension periods after knockouts and technical knockouts — treat these as minimums, not targets, and extend generously

display_text: Suspect concussion after any blow to the head, face, neck, or body that transmits force to the head, if any of the following appear: / Symptoms: headache, pressure in the head, dizziness, nausea, blurred or double vision, sensitivity to light or noise, feeling “slowed down,” “in a fog,” “not right,” difficulty concentrating or remembering, fatigue, irritability, emotional lability, sleep disturbance. / Signs: loss of consciousness (in only a minority of concussions), blank or vacant look, lying motionless, slow to get up, unsteadiness, disorientation, confusion, inability to respond appropriately, facial injury with any of the above, seizure, tonic posturing. / Immediate red flags requiring emergency evaluation: neck pain or tenderness, double vision, weakness or tingling in limbs, severe or increasing headache, seizure, loss of consciousness, deteriorating consciousness, vomiting, increasing restlessness or agitation.

display_text: The Amsterdam 2023 international consensus statement (Patricios et al., 2023, *BJSM* — the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport) provides the current framework, including an updated staged return-to-play protocol and updated assessment tools (SCAT6, Child SCAT6, SCOAT6, CRT6). The consensus organizes clinical management around a framework of “R”s — Recognize, Reduce, Remove, Re-evaluate, (Relative) Rest, Rehabilitate, Refer, Recover, Return-to-Learn/Return-to-Sport, Reconsider, Refine, and Retire — the last two being additions in the Amsterdam statement. / The staged progression, adapted for boxing: / | Stage | Activity | Boxing content | Criteria to progress | / | 1 | Symptom-limited activity | Daily activities that do not exacerbate symptoms; light walking | Tolerated without symptom exacerbation | / | 2 | Light aerobic exercise | Walking, stationary bike at low intensity | 24 h symptom-free at this level | / | 3 | Sport-specific exercise, no head impact | Shadow boxing, footwork, light bag work, running | 24 h symptom-free | / | 4 | Non-contact training drills | Full technical training, pads, bag work at normal intensity, conditioning, strength training | 24 h symptom-free | / | 5 | Full contact practice — requires medical clearance | Return to sparring, beginning at Stage 3–4 of the sparring continuum, not at the level you left | Medical clearance obtained; no symptoms | / | 6 | Return to competition | Normal competitive activity | All above cleared | / Rules: - Each stage requires at least 24 hours symptom-free before progressing - Any symptom recurrence returns the athlete to the previous stage - Stage 5 requires medical clearance, without exception - On return to sparring, drop back two stages of the sparring continuum and rebuild. Returning directly to hard sparring after a concussion is how second injuries happen - Most jurisdictions impose mandatory suspension periods after knockouts and technical knockouts — treat these as minimums, not targets, and extend generously

display_text: Diaphragmatic breathing — daily, 5–10 min - Sit or lie with one hand on the belly, one on the chest. The belly hand moves; the chest hand does not - Progress to a 4-2-6 pattern: inhale 4 s, hold 2 s, exhale 6 s. The extended exhale is the parasympathetic driver - Then practise it in the 60-second interval between rounds, on the bag and in sparring, until it is automatic. display_text: The Amsterdam 2023 international consensus statement (Patricios et al., 2023, *BJSM* — the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport) provides the current framework, including an updated staged return-to-play protocol and updated assessment tools (SCAT6, Child SCAT6, SCOAT6, CRT6). The consensus organizes clinical management around a framework of “R”s — Recognize, Reduce, Remove, Re-evaluate, (Relative) Rest, Rehabilitate, Refer, Recover, Return-to-Learn/Return-to-Sport, Reconsider, Refine, and Retire — the last two being additions in the Amsterdam statement. / The staged progression, adapted for boxing: / | Stage | Activity | Boxing content | Criteria to progress | / | 1 | Symptom-limited activity | Daily activities that do not exacerbate symptoms; light walking | Tolerated without symptom exacerbation | / | 2 | Light aerobic exercise | Walking, stationary bike at low intensity | 24 h symptom-free at this level | / | 3 | Sport-specific exercise, no head impact | Shadow boxing, footwork, light bag work, running | 24 h symptom-free | / | 4 | Non-contact training drills | Full technical training, pads, bag work at normal intensity, conditioning, strength training | 24 h symptom-free | / | 5 | Full contact practice — requires medical clearance | Return to sparring, beginning at Stage 3–4 of the sparring continuum, not at the level you left | Medical clearance obtained; no symptoms | / | 6 | Return to competition | Normal competitive activity | All above cleared | / Rules: - Each stage requires at least 24 hours symptom-free before progressing - Any symptom recurrence returns the athlete to the previous stage - Stage 5 requires medical clearance, without exception - On return to sparring, drop back two stages of the sparring continuum and rebuild. display_text: Meta-analytic work on tapering is unusually clear and unusually actionable. Bosquet et al. (2007), pooling 27 studies of competitive athletes, found: / - Overall taper effect on performance: 0.59 (moderate) / - Optimal strategy: a 2-week taper in which training volume is reduced exponentially by 41–60% (effect 0.72), with no modification of training intensity (effect 0.33 for maintained intensity) or frequency (0.35 for maintained frequency) / - Reducing intensity does not improve performance / A more recent systematic review and meta-analysis in endurance athletes (Chen et al., 2023) confirmed the pattern: reducing volume 41–60% while maintaining intensity and frequency, over ≤7 days, 8–14 days, or 15–21 days, in either a progressive or step pattern, significantly improved time-trial performance — and a taper preceded by a pre-taper overload block produced larger gains than a conventional taper. / Note also, relevant to strength retention: reduced-volume training during a taper clearly beats stopping altogether. Complete cessation for several weeks costs roughly twice the strength and velocity that maintained lower-volume training does. / Bosquet et al. display_text: Two weeks out: finalize the gameplan; begin tactical imagery of it. Reduce novelty in all life domains — this is not the week to start a new job, move house, or change your diet. / Fight week: fixed daily routine, minimal decisions, imagery of plans A, B and C. Avoid opponent-related social media and outcome-focused conversation. / Day before: weigh-in routine rehearsed and executed as practised. Light technical work. Early night. No last-minute technical changes — nothing new in the final 72 hours. / Fight day: 1. Fixed wake time, fixed meals, fixed timing — all rehearsed in camp so nothing is novel 2. Low-stimulation period: music or silence per personal preference, established months in advance, not decided on the day 3. Structured warm-up, identical every time. The ritual is doing psychological work as much as physical 4. Pre-performance routine in the final 5 minutes: breathing pattern → 3 cue words → 10-second imagery of the first exchange → physical activation 5. In the ring, between rounds: breathe first (4-2-6), then listen. Boxers who talk in the corner do not hear the corner / Post-bout: immediate physical recovery and medical check. display_text: The Amsterdam 2023 international consensus statement (Patricios et al., 2023, *BJSM* — the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport) provides the current framework, including an updated staged return-to-play protocol and updated assessment tools (SCAT6, Child SCAT6, SCOAT6, CRT6). The consensus organizes clinical management around a framework of “R”s — Recognize, Reduce, Remove, Re-evaluate, (Relative) Rest, Rehabilitate, Refer, Recover, Return-to-Learn/Return-to-Sport, Reconsider, Refine, and Retire — the last two being additions in the Amsterdam statement. / The staged progression, adapted for boxing: / | Stage | Activity | Boxing content | Criteria to progress | / | 1 | Symptom-limited activity | Daily activities that do not exacerbate symptoms; light walking | Tolerated without symptom exacerbation | / | 2 | Light aerobic exercise | Walking, stationary bike at low intensity | 24 h symptom-free at this level | / | 3 | Sport-specific exercise, no head impact | Shadow boxing, footwork, light bag work, running | 24 h symptom-free | / | 4 | Non-contact training drills | Full technical training, pads, bag work at normal intensity, conditioning, strength training | 24 h symptom-free | / | 5 | Full contact practice — requires medical clearance | Return to sparring, beginning at Stage 3–4 of the sparring continuum, not at the level you left | Medical clearance obtained; no symptoms | / | 6 | Return to competition | Normal competitive activity | All above cleared | / Rules: - Each stage requires at least 24 hours symptom-free before progressing - Any symptom recurrence returns the athlete to the previous stage - Stage 5 requires medical clearance, without exception - On return to sparring, drop back two stages of the sparring continuum and rebuild. Returning directly to hard sparring after a concussion is how second injuries happen - Most jurisdictions impose mandatory suspension periods after knockouts and technical knockouts — treat these as minimums, not targets, and extend generously

display_text: On the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR): you will encounter this metric. It divides the last 7 days’ load by a rolling ~28-day average, with the idea that a ratio around 0.8–1.3 is a “sweet spot” and spikes above ~1.5 elevate injury risk. It is intuitive and widely used, and it has been substantively criticized on methodological grounds — the mathematical coupling of numerator and denominator, arbitrary time windows, and questions about whether it predicts anything beyond simple weekly load change. Use it as a rough flag if you like it, not as a decision rule. Week-on-week load change plus monotony plus your subjective readiness data will serve you at least as well.

display_text: On the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR): you will encounter this metric. It divides the last 7 days’ load by a rolling ~28-day average, with the idea that a ratio around 0.8–1.3 is a “sweet spot” and spikes above ~1.5 elevate injury risk. It is intuitive and widely used, and it has been substantively criticized on methodological grounds — the mathematical coupling of numerator and denominator, arbitrary time windows, and questions about whether it predicts anything beyond simple weekly load change. Use it as a rough flag if you like it, not as a decision rule. Week-on-week load change plus monotony plus your subjective readiness data will serve you at least as well.

display_text: Diaphragmatic breathing — daily, 5–10 min - Sit or lie with one hand on the belly, one on the chest. The belly hand moves; the chest hand does not - Progress to a 4-2-6 pattern: inhale 4 s, hold 2 s, exhale 6 s. The extended exhale is the parasympathetic driver - Then practise it in the 60-second interval between rounds, on the bag and in sparring, until it is automatic. This is the transfer step everyone omits - Morning and pre-sleep / Progressive muscular relaxation — 2×/week, 15–20 min - Full-body protocol: tense each muscle group 5 s, release 15 s, moving systematically - Then build an abbreviated version usable in the ring: jaw, shoulders, hands — three checkpoints you can run in two seconds between exchanges / Cue words for relaxation - Anchor 2–3 words during training (“loose,” “breathe,” “long,” “soft hands”) and deploy them in competition - The anchoring matters: the word must be paired with the physical state hundreds of times in training before it will produce the state under pressure / HRV biofeedback — 3–5×/week, 10–15 min, if available - Resonance-frequency breathing training with a validated app and a chest strap - The evidence is moderate and the practice is harmless; worth doing if you will do it consistently

display_text: On the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR): you will encounter this metric. It divides the last 7 days’ load by a rolling ~28-day average, with the idea that a ratio around 0.8–1.3 is a “sweet spot” and spikes above ~1.5 elevate injury risk. It is intuitive and widely used, and it has been substantively criticized on methodological grounds — the mathematical coupling of numerator and denominator, arbitrary time windows, and questions about whether it predicts anything beyond simple weekly load change. Use it as a rough flag if you like it, not as a decision rule. Week-on-week load change plus monotony plus your subjective readiness data will serve you at least as well.

display_text: The Amsterdam 2023 international consensus statement (Patricios et al., 2023, *BJSM* — the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport) provides the current framework, including an updated staged return-to-play protocol and updated assessment tools (SCAT6, Child SCAT6, SCOAT6, CRT6). The consensus organizes clinical management around a framework of “R”s — Recognize, Reduce, Remove, Re-evaluate, (Relative) Rest, Rehabilitate, Refer, Recover, Return-to-Learn/Return-to-Sport, Reconsider, Refine, and Retire — the last two being additions in the Amsterdam statement. / The staged progression, adapted for boxing: / | Stage | Activity | Boxing content | Criteria to progress | / | 1 | Symptom-limited activity | Daily activities that do not exacerbate symptoms; light walking | Tolerated without symptom exacerbation | / | 2 | Light aerobic exercise | Walking, stationary bike at low intensity | 24 h symptom-free at this level | / | 3 | Sport-specific exercise, no head impact | Shadow boxing, footwork, light bag work, running | 24 h symptom-free | / | 4 | Non-contact training drills | Full technical training, pads, bag work at normal intensity, conditioning, strength training | 24 h symptom-free | / | 5 | Full contact practice — requires medical clearance | Return to sparring, beginning at Stage 3–4 of the sparring continuum, not at the level you left | Medical clearance obtained; no symptoms | / | 6 | Return to competition | Normal competitive activity | All above cleared | / Rules: - Each stage requires at least 24 hours symptom-free before progressing - Any symptom recurrence returns the athlete to the previous stage - Stage 5 requires medical clearance, without exception - On return to sparring, drop back two stages of the sparring continuum and rebuild. Returning directly to hard sparring after a concussion is how second injuries happen - Most jurisdictions impose mandatory suspension periods after knockouts and technical knockouts — treat these as minimums, not targets, and extend generously

display_text: The Amsterdam 2023 international consensus statement (Patricios et al., 2023, *BJSM* — the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport) provides the current framework, including an updated staged return-to-play protocol and updated assessment tools (SCAT6, Child SCAT6, SCOAT6, CRT6). display_text: The Amsterdam 2023 international consensus statement (Patricios et al., 2023, *BJSM* — the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport) provides the current framework, including an updated staged return-to-play protocol and updated assessment tools (SCAT6, Child SCAT6, SCOAT6, CRT6). The consensus organizes clinical management around a framework of “R”s — Recognize, Reduce, Remove, Re-evaluate, (Relative) Rest, Rehabilitate, Refer, Recover, Return-to-Learn/Return-to-Sport, Reconsider, Refine, and Retire — the last two being additions in the Amsterdam statement. / The staged progression, adapted for boxing: / | Stage | Activity | Boxing content | Criteria to progress | / | 1 | Symptom-limited activity | Daily activities that do not exacerbate symptoms; light walking | Tolerated without symptom exacerbation | / | 2 | Light aerobic exercise | Walking, stationary bike at low intensity | 24 h symptom-free at this level | / | 3 | Sport-specific exercise, no head impact | Shadow boxing, footwork, light bag work, running | 24 h symptom-free | / | 4 | Non-contact training drills | Full technical training, pads, bag work at normal intensity, conditioning, strength training | 24 h symptom-free | / | 5 | Full contact practice — requires medical clearance | Return to sparring, beginning at Stage 3–4 of the sparring continuum, not at the level you left | Medical clearance obtained; no symptoms | / | 6 | Return to competition | Normal competitive activity | All above cleared | / Rules: - Each stage requires at least 24 hours symptom-free before progressing - Any symptom recurrence returns the athlete to the previous stage - Stage 5 requires medical clearance, without exception - On return to sparring, drop back two stages of the sparring continuum and rebuild. Returning directly to hard sparring after a concussion is how second injuries happen - Most jurisdictions impose mandatory suspension periods after knockouts and technical knockouts — treat these as minimums, not targets, and extend generously

display_text: Diaphragmatic breathing — daily, 5–10 min - Sit or lie with one hand on the belly, one on the chest. The belly hand moves; the chest hand does not - Progress to a 4-2-6 pattern: inhale 4 s, hold 2 s, exhale 6 s. The extended exhale is the parasympathetic driver - Then practise it in the 60-second interval between rounds, on the bag and in sparring, until it is automatic. This is the transfer step everyone omits - Morning and pre-sleep / Progressive muscular relaxation — 2×/week, 15–20 min - Full-body protocol: tense each muscle group 5 s, release 15 s, moving systematically - Then build an abbreviated version usable in the ring: jaw, shoulders, hands — three checkpoints you can run in two seconds between exchanges / Cue words for relaxation - Anchor 2–3 words during training (“loose,” “breathe,” “long,” “soft hands”) and deploy them in competition - The anchoring matters: the word must be paired with the physical state hundreds of times in training before it will produce the state under pressure / HRV biofeedback — 3–5×/week, 10–15 min, if available - Resonance-frequency breathing training with a validated app and a chest strap - The evidence is moderate and the practice is harmless; worth doing if you will do it consistently

display_text: Diaphragmatic breathing — daily, 5–10 min - Sit or lie with one hand on the belly, one on the chest. display_text: Sparring block (55 min) - Format matched to competition exactly: 3 × 3 min for elite amateur, or the professional distance, with 1-min intervals and a real corner. Same gloves, same headgear spec, same wraps - Rounds 1–3: full competition simulation against the opponent-emulating partner. The coach corners as they would in competition — 1-minute corner instructions only, no talking during rounds. This matters: boxers coached continuously during sparring cannot function in a bout where instruction is limited to 60 seconds - Break, 5 min: structured debrief. What happened? What did they give you? What did you miss? What will you do differently? - Rounds 4–6: second partner, different problem. Impose a specific bout scenario — “you are two points down going into the last round,” or “your opponent has just hurt you and you have 90 seconds to survive and recover” - Rounds 7–9 (if prescribed): technical rounds at 50–60%, focusing on the one thing that failed above

display_text: 2. Long slow distance running is an inefficient tool for aerobic development in an already-trained athlete, and it interferes with power development. It has legitimate roles — early tissue conditioning, recovery, capillarization, psychological discipline — but the aerobic ceiling is raised far more efficiently by interval work. The concurrent training literature adds a further reason to limit running specifically: running produces more interference with strength adaptation than cycling, likely via eccentric loading and muscle damage.

display_text: The IOC consensus statement on dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete (Maughan et al., 2018) identified a short list with adequate evidence for performance benefit: caffeine, creatine monohydrate, nitrate, sodium bicarbonate, and possibly β-alanine. It also emphasized that performance supplements should be considered only where a strong evidence base supports them as safe, legal and effective, ideally after adequacy of dietary practice is ensured, and that they should be trialled thoroughly in training that mimics competition before use in competition. / | Supplement | Evidence | Boxing relevance | Dosing | Practical notes | / | Creatine monohydrate | Strong | High — repeated high-intensity efforts, strength and power development, possible cognitive interest | 3–5 g/day continuously; optional 20 g/day loading × 5–7 days | Causes ~1–2 kg water-weight gain. Start it in the off-season, not in camp. Monohydrate only — the exotic forms have no advantage | / | Caffeine | Strong | High — reduces perceived exertion, improves alertness, reaction time and power output | 3–6 mg/kg, 45–60 min pre-competition | Trial in training first. Beware sleep disruption and over-arousal in an already anxious athlete. Habitual high intake blunts the acute effect | / | Sodium bicarbonate | Good, with high individual variability | Moderate-high — extracellular buffering for exactly the acidosis boxing produces | 0.2–0.3 g/kg, 60–150 min pre-event, or split-dose protocols | GI distress is common and can ruin a performance. Must be trialled extensively. Split doses and enteric-coated forms reduce this | / | β-alanine | Reasonable | Moderate — intramuscular carnosine buffering | 3.2–6.4 g/day in divided doses for 4+ weeks | Loading is cumulative, not acute — no point taking it on fight day. Paraesthesia (harmless tingling) is common; divided doses reduce it | / | Dietary nitrate (beetroot) | Good for medium-duration endurance | Low-moderate for boxing specifically | 6–8 mmol nitrate, 2–3 h pre-event | Avoid antibacterial mouthwash, which disrupts the oral bacteria needed for conversion | / | Protein powder | Convenience, not magic | Useful | To meet daily protein targets when whole food is impractical | Whey, casein, or plant blends — all work | / | Vitamin D | Strong if deficient | Correct deficiency; do not supplement blind | Per blood results | Common deficiency in northern latitudes and indoor athletes | / | Iron | Strong if deficient | Correct deficiency; do not supplement blind | Per blood results and medical guidance | Higher priority for female boxers and high running volumes. Do not take iron without a blood test — excess is harmful | / | Everything else — fat burners, testosterone boosters, BCAAs in a protein-sufficient diet, “nootropic” blends, most pre-workouts, collagen for punch power, exotic creatine forms | Weak or absent | Low | — | Not recommended |

display_text: The Amsterdam 2023 international consensus statement (Patricios et al., 2023, *BJSM* — the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport) provides the current framework, including an updated staged return-to-play protocol and updated assessment tools (SCAT6, Child SCAT6, SCOAT6, CRT6). The consensus organizes clinical management around a framework of “R”s — Recognize, Reduce, Remove, Re-evaluate, (Relative) Rest, Rehabilitate, Refer, Recover, Return-to-Learn/Return-to-Sport, Reconsider, Refine, and Retire — the last two being additions in the Amsterdam statement. / The staged progression, adapted for boxing: / | Stage | Activity | Boxing content | Criteria to progress | / | 1 | Symptom-limited activity | Daily activities that do not exacerbate symptoms; light walking | Tolerated without symptom exacerbation | / | 2 | Light aerobic exercise | Walking, stationary bike at low intensity | 24 h symptom-free at this level | / | 3 | Sport-specific exercise, no head impact | Shadow boxing, footwork, light bag work, running | 24 h symptom-free | / | 4 | Non-contact training drills | Full technical training, pads, bag work at normal intensity, conditioning, strength training | 24 h symptom-free | / | 5 | Full contact practice — requires medical clearance | Return to sparring, beginning at Stage 3–4 of the sparring continuum, not at the level you left | Medical clearance obtained; no symptoms | / | 6 | Return to competition | Normal competitive activity | All above cleared | / Rules: - Each stage requires at least 24 hours symptom-free before progressing - Any symptom recurrence returns the athlete to the previous stage - Stage 5 requires medical clearance, without exception - On return to sparring, drop back two stages of the sparring continuum and rebuild. display_text: Diaphragmatic breathing — daily, 5–10 min - Sit or lie with one hand on the belly, one on the chest. The belly hand moves; the chest hand does not - Progress to a 4-2-6 pattern: inhale 4 s, hold 2 s, exhale 6 s. The extended exhale is the parasympathetic driver - Then practise it in the 60-second interval between rounds, on the bag and in sparring, until it is automatic. This is the transfer step everyone omits - Morning and pre-sleep / Progressive muscular relaxation — 2×/week, 15–20 min - Full-body protocol: tense each muscle group 5 s, release 15 s, moving systematically - Then build an abbreviated version usable in the ring: jaw, shoulders, hands — three checkpoints you can run in two seconds between exchanges / Cue words for relaxation - Anchor 2–3 words during training (“loose,” “breathe,” “long,” “soft hands”) and deploy them in competition - The anchoring matters: the word must be paired with the physical state hundreds of times in training before it will produce the state under pressure / HRV biofeedback — 3–5×/week, 10–15 min, if available - Resonance-frequency breathing training with a validated app and a chest strap - The evidence is moderate and the practice is harmless; worth doing if you will do it consistently

display_text: Suspect concussion after any blow to the head, face, neck, or body that transmits force to the head, if any of the following appear: / Symptoms: headache, pressure in the head, dizziness, nausea, blurred or double vision, sensitivity to light or noise, feeling “slowed down,” “in a fog,” “not right,” difficulty concentrating or remembering, fatigue, irritability, emotional lability, sleep disturbance. / Signs: loss of consciousness (in only a minority of concussions), blank or vacant look, lying motionless, slow to get up, unsteadiness, disorientation, confusion, inability to respond appropriately, facial injury with any of the above, seizure, tonic posturing. / Immediate red flags requiring emergency evaluation: neck pain or tenderness, double vision, weakness or tingling in limbs, severe or increasing headache, seizure, loss of consciousness, deteriorating consciousness, vomiting, increasing restlessness or agitation.

display_text: Menstrual cycle tracking as a monitoring variable. Track alongside training load — symptoms, cycle day, and subjective performance. Individual patterns are far more useful than population generalizations. / On phase-based training periodization, be sceptical. A systematic review of menstrual cycle effects on elite athlete performance found that of 662 papers reviewed and 218 assessed for eligibility, only seven precisely investigated a performance parameter across at least one cycle phase in elite athletes — and concluded that while various parameters are affected, the parameters themselves and the magnitude and direction of effects are inconclusive (Meignié et al., 2021). A more recent review in the strength and conditioning literature stated the position plainly: research does not currently support the idea that periodizing strength or endurance training according to the menstrual cycle confers additional benefit over traditional approaches. / Practical position: track the cycle, learn *your own* patterns, adjust individually based on your data, and do not adopt a rigid phase-based template on the basis of social media claims. If you consistently perform worse or feel worse in a particular phase, that is real for you and worth accommodating.

display_text: Diaphragmatic breathing — daily, 5–10 min - Sit or lie with one hand on the belly, one on the chest. The belly hand moves; the chest hand does not - Progress to a 4-2-6 pattern: inhale 4 s, hold 2 s, exhale 6 s. The extended exhale is the parasympathetic driver - Then practise it in the 60-second interval between rounds, on the bag and in sparring, until it is automatic. display_text: Menstrual cycle tracking as a monitoring variable. Track alongside training load — symptoms, cycle day, and subjective performance. Individual patterns are far more useful than population generalizations. / On phase-based training periodization, be sceptical. A systematic review of menstrual cycle effects on elite athlete performance found that of 662 papers reviewed and 218 assessed for eligibility, only seven precisely investigated a performance parameter across at least one cycle phase in elite athletes — and concluded that while various parameters are affected, the parameters themselves and the magnitude and direction of effects are inconclusive (Meignié et al., 2021). A more recent review in the strength and conditioning literature stated the position plainly: research does not currently support the idea that periodizing strength or endurance training according to the menstrual cycle confers additional benefit over traditional approaches. / Practical position: track the cycle, learn *your own* patterns, adjust individually based on your data, and do not adopt a rigid phase-based template on the basis of social media claims. If you consistently perform worse or feel worse in a particular phase, that is real for you and worth accommodating.

display_text: On the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR): you will encounter this metric. It divides the last 7 days’ load by a rolling ~28-day average, with the idea that a ratio around 0.8–1.3 is a “sweet spot” and spikes above ~1.5 elevate injury risk. It is intuitive and widely used, and it has been substantively criticized on methodological grounds — the mathematical coupling of numerator and denominator, arbitrary time windows, and questions about whether it predicts anything beyond simple weekly load change. Use it as a rough flag if you like it, not as a decision rule. Week-on-week load change plus monotony plus your subjective readiness data will serve you at least as well.

display_text: Two weeks out: finalize the gameplan; begin tactical imagery of it. Reduce novelty in all life domains — this is not the week to start a new job, move house, or change your diet. / Fight week: fixed daily routine, minimal decisions, imagery of plans A, B and C. Avoid opponent-related social media and outcome-focused conversation. / Day before: weigh-in routine rehearsed and executed as practised. Light technical work. Early night. No last-minute technical changes — nothing new in the final 72 hours. / Fight day: 1. Fixed wake time, fixed meals, fixed timing — all rehearsed in camp so nothing is novel 2. Low-stimulation period: music or silence per personal preference, established months in advance, not decided on the day 3. Structured warm-up, identical every time. The ritual is doing psychological work as much as physical 4. Pre-performance routine in the final 5 minutes: breathing pattern → 3 cue words → 10-second imagery of the first exchange → physical activation 5. In the ring, between rounds: breathe first (4-2-6), then listen. Boxers who talk in the corner do not hear the corner / Post-bout: immediate physical recovery and medical check. No tactical analysis for 24–48 hours. Then structured video review against the Part 2 §4 KPIs, one technical fix, one tactical fix, one documented lesson.

display_text: Meta-analytic work on tapering is unusually clear and unusually actionable. Bosquet et al. (2007), pooling 27 studies of competitive athletes, found: / - Overall taper effect on performance: 0.59 (moderate) / - Optimal strategy: a 2-week taper in which training volume is reduced exponentially by 41–60% (effect 0.72), with no modification of training intensity (effect 0.33 for maintained intensity) or frequency (0.35 for maintained frequency) / - Reducing intensity does not improve performance / A more recent systematic review and meta-analysis in endurance athletes (Chen et al., 2023) confirmed the pattern: reducing volume 41–60% while maintaining intensity and frequency, over ≤7 days, 8–14 days, or 15–21 days, in either a progressive or step pattern, significantly improved time-trial performance — and a taper preceded by a pre-taper overload block produced larger gains than a conventional taper. / Note also, relevant to strength retention: reduced-volume training during a taper clearly beats stopping altogether. Complete cessation for several weeks costs roughly twice the strength and velocity that maintained lower-volume training does. / Bosquet et al. (2007), meta-analysis of 27 studies of competitive athletes: - Overall taper effect on performance: 0.59 - Optimal: 2-week taper, volume reduced exponentially by 41–60% (effect 0.72), intensity unchanged (0.33 for maintained), frequency unchanged (0.35 for maintained) - Reducing intensity does not improve performance

display_text: On the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR): you will encounter this metric. It divides the last 7 days’ load by a rolling ~28-day average, with the idea that a ratio around 0.8–1.3 is a “sweet spot” and spikes above ~1.5 elevate injury risk. It is intuitive and widely used, and it has been substantively criticized on methodological grounds — the mathematical coupling of numerator and denominator, arbitrary time windows, and questions about whether it predicts anything beyond simple weekly load change. Use it as a rough flag if you like it, not as a decision rule. Week-on-week load change plus monotony plus your subjective readiness data will serve you at least as well.

display_text: Two weeks out: finalize the gameplan; begin tactical imagery of it. Reduce novelty in all life domains — this is not the week to start a new job, move house, or change your diet. / Fight week: fixed daily routine, minimal decisions, imagery of plans A, B and C. Avoid opponent-related social media and outcome-focused conversation. / Day before: weigh-in routine rehearsed and executed as practised. Light technical work. Early night. No last-minute technical changes — nothing new in the final 72 hours. / Fight day: 1. Fixed wake time, fixed meals, fixed timing — all rehearsed in camp so nothing is novel 2. Low-stimulation period: music or silence per personal preference, established months in advance, not decided on the day 3. Structured warm-up, identical every time. The ritual is doing psychological work as much as physical 4. Pre-performance routine in the final 5 minutes: breathing pattern → 3 cue words → 10-second imagery of the first exchange → physical activation 5. display_text: Diaphragmatic breathing — daily, 5–10 min - Sit or lie with one hand on the belly, one on the chest. The belly hand moves; the chest hand does not - Progress to a 4-2-6 pattern: inhale 4 s, hold 2 s, exhale 6 s. The extended exhale is the parasympathetic driver - Then practise it in the 60-second interval between rounds, on the bag and in sparring, until it is automatic. This is the transfer step everyone omits - Morning and pre-sleep / Progressive muscular relaxation — 2×/week, 15–20 min - Full-body protocol: tense each muscle group 5 s, release 15 s, moving systematically - Then build an abbreviated version usable in the ring: jaw, shoulders, hands — three checkpoints you can run in two seconds between exchanges / Cue words for relaxation - Anchor 2–3 words during training (“loose,” “breathe,” “long,” “soft hands”) and deploy them in competition - The anchoring matters: the word must be paired with the physical state hundreds of times in training before it will produce the state under pressure / HRV biofeedback — 3–5×/week, 10–15 min, if available - Resonance-frequency breathing training with a validated app and a chest strap - The evidence is moderate and the practice is harmless; worth doing if you will do it consistently

display_text: The Amsterdam 2023 international consensus statement (Patricios et al., 2023, *BJSM* — the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport) provides the current framework, including an updated staged return-to-play protocol and updated assessment tools (SCAT6, Child SCAT6, SCOAT6, CRT6). The consensus organizes clinical management around a framework of “R”s — Recognize, Reduce, Remove, Re-evaluate, (Relative) Rest, Rehabilitate, Refer, Recover, Return-to-Learn/Return-to-Sport, Reconsider, Refine, and Retire — the last two being additions in the Amsterdam statement. / The staged progression, adapted for boxing: / | Stage | Activity | Boxing content | Criteria to progress | / | 1 | Symptom-limited activity | Daily activities that do not exacerbate symptoms; light walking | Tolerated without symptom exacerbation | / | 2 | Light aerobic exercise | Walking, stationary bike at low intensity | 24 h symptom-free at this level | / | 3 | Sport-specific exercise, no head impact | Shadow boxing, footwork, light bag work, running | 24 h symptom-free | / | 4 | Non-contact training drills | Full technical training, pads, bag work at normal intensity, conditioning, strength training | 24 h symptom-free | / | 5 | Full contact practice — requires medical clearance | Return to sparring, beginning at Stage 3–4 of the sparring continuum, not at the level you left | Medical clearance obtained; no symptoms | / | 6 | Return to competition | Normal competitive activity | All above cleared | / Rules: - Each stage requires at least 24 hours symptom-free before progressing - Any symptom recurrence returns the athlete to the previous stage - Stage 5 requires medical clearance, without exception - On return to sparring, drop back two stages of the sparring continuum and rebuild. Returning directly to hard sparring after a concussion is how second injuries happen - Most jurisdictions impose mandatory suspension periods after knockouts and technical knockouts — treat these as minimums, not targets, and extend generously

display_text: Menstrual cycle tracking as a monitoring variable. Track alongside training load — symptoms, cycle day, and subjective performance. display_text: Diaphragmatic breathing — daily, 5–10 min - Sit or lie with one hand on the belly, one on the chest. The belly hand moves; the chest hand does not - Progress to a 4-2-6 pattern: inhale 4 s, hold 2 s, exhale 6 s. display_text: Standardization rules that make the difference between data and noise: - Same time of day (±1 hour), same order, same equipment, same surface, same footwear - Same warm-up protocol, written down and followed exactly - At least 48 hours after hard training, never after sparring - Not in a state of acute weight loss - Three attempts on power tests, take the best; report all three so you can see variability - Record body mass at the same time, because most results are interpreted relative to it

display_text: Menstrual cycle tracking as a monitoring variable. Track alongside training load — symptoms, cycle day, and subjective performance. Individual patterns are far more useful than population generalizations. / On phase-based training periodization, be sceptical. A systematic review of menstrual cycle effects on elite athlete performance found that of 662 papers reviewed and 218 assessed for eligibility, only seven precisely investigated a performance parameter across at least one cycle phase in elite athletes — and concluded that while various parameters are affected, the parameters themselves and the magnitude and direction of effects are inconclusive (Meignié et al., 2021). A more recent review in the strength and conditioning literature stated the position plainly: research does not currently support the idea that periodizing strength or endurance training according to the menstrual cycle confers additional benefit over traditional approaches. / Practical position: track the cycle, learn *your own* patterns, adjust individually based on your data, and do not adopt a rigid phase-based template on the basis of social media claims. If you consistently perform worse or feel worse in a particular phase, that is real for you and worth accommodating.

display_text: Two weeks out: finalize the gameplan; begin tactical imagery of it. Reduce novelty in all life domains — this is not the week to start a new job, move house, or change your diet. / Fight week: fixed daily routine, minimal decisions, imagery of plans A, B and C. Avoid opponent-related social media and outcome-focused conversation. / Day before: weigh-in routine rehearsed and executed as practised. Light technical work. Early night. No last-minute technical changes — nothing new in the final 72 hours. / Fight day: 1. Fixed wake time, fixed meals, fixed timing — all rehearsed in camp so nothing is novel 2. Low-stimulation period: music or silence per personal preference, established months in advance, not decided on the day 3. Structured warm-up, identical every time. The ritual is doing psychological work as much as physical 4. Pre-performance routine in the final 5 minutes: breathing pattern → 3 cue words → 10-second imagery of the first exchange → physical activation 5. In the ring, between rounds: breathe first (4-2-6), then listen. Boxers who talk in the corner do not hear the corner / Post-bout: immediate physical recovery and medical check. No tactical analysis for 24–48 hours. Then structured video review against the Part 2 §4 KPIs, one technical fix, one tactical fix, one documented lesson.

display_text: The Amsterdam 2023 international consensus statement (Patricios et al., 2023, *BJSM* — the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport) provides the current framework, including an updated staged return-to-play protocol and updated assessment tools (SCAT6, Child SCAT6, SCOAT6, CRT6). The consensus organizes clinical management around a framework of “R”s — Recognize, Reduce, Remove, Re-evaluate, (Relative) Rest, Rehabilitate, Refer, Recover, Return-to-Learn/Return-to-Sport, Reconsider, Refine, and Retire — the last two being additions in the Amsterdam statement. / The staged progression, adapted for boxing: / | Stage | Activity | Boxing content | Criteria to progress | / | 1 | Symptom-limited activity | Daily activities that do not exacerbate symptoms; light walking | Tolerated without symptom exacerbation | / | 2 | Light aerobic exercise | Walking, stationary bike at low intensity | 24 h symptom-free at this level | / | 3 | Sport-specific exercise, no head impact | Shadow boxing, footwork, light bag work, running | 24 h symptom-free | / | 4 | Non-contact training drills | Full technical training, pads, bag work at normal intensity, conditioning, strength training | 24 h symptom-free | / | 5 | Full contact practice — requires medical clearance | Return to sparring, beginning at Stage 3–4 of the sparring continuum, not at the level you left | Medical clearance obtained; no symptoms | / | 6 | Return to competition | Normal competitive activity | All above cleared | / Rules: - Each stage requires at least 24 hours symptom-free before progressing - Any symptom recurrence returns the athlete to the previous stage - Stage 5 requires medical clearance, without exception - On return to sparring, drop back two stages of the sparring continuum and rebuild. Returning directly to hard sparring after a concussion is how second injuries happen - Most jurisdictions impose mandatory suspension periods after knockouts and technical knockouts — treat these as minimums, not targets, and extend generously

display_text: Menstrual cycle tracking as a monitoring variable. Track alongside training load — symptoms, cycle day, and subjective performance. Individual patterns are far more useful than population generalizations. / On phase-based training periodization, be sceptical. A systematic review of menstrual cycle effects on elite athlete performance found that of 662 papers reviewed and 218 assessed for eligibility, only seven precisely investigated a performance parameter across at least one cycle phase in elite athletes — and concluded that while various parameters are affected, the parameters themselves and the magnitude and direction of effects are inconclusive (Meignié et al., 2021). A more recent review in the strength and conditioning literature stated the position plainly: research does not currently support the idea that periodizing strength or endurance training according to the menstrual cycle confers additional benefit over traditional approaches. / Practical position: track the cycle, learn *your own* patterns, adjust individually based on your data, and do not adopt a rigid phase-based template on the basis of social media claims. If you consistently perform worse or feel worse in a particular phase, that is real for you and worth accommodating.

display_text: On the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR): you will encounter this metric. It divides the last 7 days’ load by a rolling ~28-day average, with the idea that a ratio around 0.8–1.3 is a “sweet spot” and spikes above ~1.5 elevate injury risk. It is intuitive and widely used, and it has been substantively criticized on methodological grounds — the mathematical coupling of numerator and denominator, arbitrary time windows, and questions about whether it predicts anything beyond simple weekly load change. Use it as a rough flag if you like it, not as a decision rule. Week-on-week load change plus monotony plus your subjective readiness data will serve you at least as well.

display_text: The Amsterdam 2023 international consensus statement (Patricios et al., 2023, *BJSM* — the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport) provides the current framework, including an updated staged return-to-play protocol and updated assessment tools (SCAT6, Child SCAT6, SCOAT6, CRT6). The consensus organizes clinical management around a framework of “R”s — Recognize, Reduce, Remove, Re-evaluate, (Relative) Rest, Rehabilitate, Refer, Recover, Return-to-Learn/Return-to-Sport, Reconsider, Refine, and Retire — the last two being additions in the Amsterdam statement. / The staged progression, adapted for boxing: / | Stage | Activity | Boxing content | Criteria to progress | / | 1 | Symptom-limited activity | Daily activities that do not exacerbate symptoms; light walking | Tolerated without symptom exacerbation | / | 2 | Light aerobic exercise | Walking, stationary bike at low intensity | 24 h symptom-free at this level | / | 3 | Sport-specific exercise, no head impact | Shadow boxing, footwork, light bag work, running | 24 h symptom-free | / | 4 | Non-contact training drills | Full technical training, pads, bag work at normal intensity, conditioning, strength training | 24 h symptom-free | / | 5 | Full contact practice — requires medical clearance | Return to sparring, beginning at Stage 3–4 of the sparring continuum, not at the level you left | Medical clearance obtained; no symptoms | / | 6 | Return to competition | Normal competitive activity | All above cleared | / Rules: - Each stage requires at least 24 hours symptom-free before progressing - Any symptom recurrence returns the athlete to the previous stage - Stage 5 requires medical clearance, without exception - On return to sparring, drop back two stages of the sparring continuum and rebuild. Returning directly to hard sparring after a concussion is how second injuries happen - Most jurisdictions impose mandatory suspension periods after knockouts and technical knockouts — treat these as minimums, not targets, and extend generously

display_text: From notational analysis of elite women’s World Championship finals: pivoting and shifting back, particularly when followed by counterattack, were significantly associated with winning, while parrying and single counterpunches were associated with losing. display_text: Meta-analytic work on tapering is unusually clear and unusually actionable. Bosquet et al. (2007), pooling 27 studies of competitive athletes, found: / - Overall taper effect on performance: 0.59 (moderate) / - Optimal strategy: a 2-week taper in which training volume is reduced exponentially by 41–60% (effect 0.72), with no modification of training intensity (effect 0.33 for maintained intensity) or frequency (0.35 for maintained frequency) / - Reducing intensity does not improve performance / A more recent systematic review and meta-analysis in endurance athletes (Chen et al., 2023) confirmed the pattern: reducing volume 41–60% while maintaining intensity and frequency, over ≤7 days, 8–14 days, or 15–21 days, in either a progressive or step pattern, significantly improved time-trial performance — and a taper preceded by a pre-taper overload block produced larger gains than a conventional taper. / Note also, relevant to strength retention: reduced-volume training during a taper clearly beats stopping altogether. display_text: Menstrual cycle tracking as a monitoring variable. Track alongside training load — symptoms, cycle day, and subjective performance. Individual patterns are far more useful than population generalizations. / On phase-based training periodization, be sceptical. A systematic review of menstrual cycle effects on elite athlete performance found that of 662 papers reviewed and 218 assessed for eligibility, only seven precisely investigated a performance parameter across at least one cycle phase in elite athletes — and concluded that while various parameters are affected, the parameters themselves and the magnitude and direction of effects are inconclusive (Meignié et al., 2021). display_text: Diaphragmatic breathing — daily, 5–10 min - Sit or lie with one hand on the belly, one on the chest. The belly hand moves; the chest hand does not - Progress to a 4-2-6 pattern: inhale 4 s, hold 2 s, exhale 6 s. The extended exhale is the parasympathetic driver - Then practise it in the 60-second interval between rounds, on the bag and in sparring, until it is automatic. This is the transfer step everyone omits - Morning and pre-sleep / Progressive muscular relaxation — 2×/week, 15–20 min - Full-body protocol: tense each muscle group 5 s, release 15 s, moving systematically - Then build an abbreviated version usable in the ring: jaw, shoulders, hands — three checkpoints you can run in two seconds between exchanges / Cue words for relaxation - Anchor 2–3 words during training (“loose,” “breathe,” “long,” “soft hands”) and deploy them in competition - The anchoring matters: the word must be paired with the physical state hundreds of times in training before it will produce the state under pressure / HRV biofeedback — 3–5×/week, 10–15 min, if available - Resonance-frequency breathing training with a validated app and a chest strap - The evidence is moderate and the practice is harmless; worth doing if you will do it consistently

display_text: The IOC consensus statement on dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete (Maughan et al., 2018) identified a short list with adequate evidence for performance benefit: caffeine, creatine monohydrate, nitrate, sodium bicarbonate, and possibly β-alanine. It also emphasized that performance supplements should be considered only where a strong evidence base supports them as safe, legal and effective, ideally after adequacy of dietary practice is ensured, and that they should be trialled thoroughly in training that mimics competition before use in competition. / | Supplement | Evidence | Boxing relevance | Dosing | Practical notes | / | Creatine monohydrate | Strong | High — repeated high-intensity efforts, strength and power development, possible cognitive interest | 3–5 g/day continuously; optional 20 g/day loading × 5–7 days | Causes ~1–2 kg water-weight gain. Start it in the off-season, not in camp. Monohydrate only — the exotic forms have no advantage | / | Caffeine | Strong | High — reduces perceived exertion, improves alertness, reaction time and power output | 3–6 mg/kg, 45–60 min pre-competition | Trial in training first. Beware sleep disruption and over-arousal in an already anxious athlete. Habitual high intake blunts the acute effect | / | Sodium bicarbonate | Good, with high individual variability | Moderate-high — extracellular buffering for exactly the acidosis boxing produces | 0.2–0.3 g/kg, 60–150 min pre-event, or split-dose protocols | GI distress is common and can ruin a performance. Must be trialled extensively. display_text: The Amsterdam 2023 international consensus statement (Patricios et al., 2023, *BJSM* — the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport) provides the current framework, including an updated staged return-to-play protocol and updated assessment tools (SCAT6, Child SCAT6, SCOAT6, CRT6). The consensus organizes clinical management around a framework of “R”s — Recognize, Reduce, Remove, Re-evaluate, (Relative) Rest, Rehabilitate, Refer, Recover, Return-to-Learn/Return-to-Sport, Reconsider, Refine, and Retire — the last two being additions in the Amsterdam statement. / The staged progression, adapted for boxing: / | Stage | Activity | Boxing content | Criteria to progress | / | 1 | Symptom-limited activity | Daily activities that do not exacerbate symptoms; light walking | Tolerated without symptom exacerbation | / | 2 | Light aerobic exercise | Walking, stationary bike at low intensity | 24 h symptom-free at this level | / | 3 | Sport-specific exercise, no head impact | Shadow boxing, footwork, light bag work, running | 24 h symptom-free | / | 4 | Non-contact training drills | Full technical training, pads, bag work at normal intensity, conditioning, strength training | 24 h symptom-free | / | 5 | Full contact practice — requires medical clearance | Return to sparring, beginning at Stage 3–4 of the sparring continuum, not at the level you left | Medical clearance obtained; no symptoms | / | 6 | Return to competition | Normal competitive activity | All above cleared | / Rules: - Each stage requires at least 24 hours symptom-free before progressing - Any symptom recurrence returns the athlete to the previous stage - Stage 5 requires medical clearance, without exception - On return to sparring, drop back two stages of the sparring continuum and rebuild. Returning directly to hard sparring after a concussion is how second injuries happen - Most jurisdictions impose mandatory suspension periods after knockouts and technical knockouts — treat these as minimums, not targets, and extend generously

display_text: 2. Long slow distance running is an inefficient tool for aerobic development in an already-trained athlete, and it interferes with power development. It has legitimate roles — early tissue conditioning, recovery, capillarization, psychological discipline — but the aerobic ceiling is raised far more efficiently by interval work. The concurrent training literature adds a further reason to limit running specifically: running produces more interference with strength adaptation than cycling, likely via eccentric loading and muscle damage.

display_text: The Amsterdam 2023 international consensus statement (Patricios et al., 2023, *BJSM* — the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport) provides the current framework, including an updated staged return-to-play protocol and updated assessment tools (SCAT6, Child SCAT6, SCOAT6, CRT6). The consensus organizes clinical management around a framework of “R”s — Recognize, Reduce, Remove, Re-evaluate, (Relative) Rest, Rehabilitate, Refer, Recover, Return-to-Learn/Return-to-Sport, Reconsider, Refine, and Retire — the last two being additions in the Amsterdam statement. / The staged progression, adapted for boxing: / | Stage | Activity | Boxing content | Criteria to progress | / | 1 | Symptom-limited activity | Daily activities that do not exacerbate symptoms; light walking | Tolerated without symptom exacerbation | / | 2 | Light aerobic exercise | Walking, stationary bike at low intensity | 24 h symptom-free at this level | / | 3 | Sport-specific exercise, no head impact | Shadow boxing, footwork, light bag work, running | 24 h symptom-free | / | 4 | Non-contact training drills | Full technical training, pads, bag work at normal intensity, conditioning, strength training | 24 h symptom-free | / | 5 | Full contact practice — requires medical clearance | Return to sparring, beginning at Stage 3–4 of the sparring continuum, not at the level you left | Medical clearance obtained; no symptoms | / | 6 | Return to competition | Normal competitive activity | All above cleared | / Rules: - Each stage requires at least 24 hours symptom-free before progressing - Any symptom recurrence returns the athlete to the previous stage - Stage 5 requires medical clearance, without exception - On return to sparring, drop back two stages of the sparring continuum and rebuild. Returning directly to hard sparring after a concussion is how second injuries happen - Most jurisdictions impose mandatory suspension periods after knockouts and technical knockouts — treat these as minimums, not targets, and extend generously

display_text: From notational analysis of elite women’s World Championship finals: pivoting and shifting back, particularly when followed by counterattack, were significantly associated with winning, while parrying and single counterpunches were associated with losing. Defensive effectiveness ratios also favored winners. / Earlier work found that defensive movements are most valuable when they initiate a counterattack rather than merely avoiding. / The instruction that follows: dynamic, mobile, offensive defense wins. Static, reactive, hand-based defense loses. And isolated single counters lose — the counter needs to be the start of something.

display_text: When to have the first bout. Not at a fixed date — when these are all true: 1. 12+ weeks of controlled two-way sparring with multiple partners 2. Get taught by someone competent and practise until consistent. Bad wrapping causes injuries | / | Punching mechanics review | Most hand injuries have a technique component — landing on the wrong knuckles, wrist extension at impact, poor alignment. Slow-motion video of bag work reveals this immediately and almost nobody does it | / | Progressive bag loading | Do not go from nothing to full-power heavy bag rounds. Build over months | / | Grip, forearm and wrist strengthening | Heavy carries, wrist rollers, rice-bucket work, isometric grip holds, wrist extension band work | / | Report knuckle pain and swelling early | Boxer’s knuckle progresses. display_text: Two weeks out: finalize the gameplan; begin tactical imagery of it. Reduce novelty in all life domains — this is not the week to start a new job, move house, or change your diet. / Fight week: fixed daily routine, minimal decisions, imagery of plans A, B and C. Avoid opponent-related social media and outcome-focused conversation. / Day before: weigh-in routine rehearsed and executed as practised. Light technical work. Early night. No last-minute technical changes — nothing new in the final 72 hours. / Fight day: 1. Fixed wake time, fixed meals, fixed timing — all rehearsed in camp so nothing is novel 2. Low-stimulation period: music or silence per personal preference, established months in advance, not decided on the day 3. Structured warm-up, identical every time. The ritual is doing psychological work as much as physical 4. Pre-performance routine in the final 5 minutes: breathing pattern → 3 cue words → 10-second imagery of the first exchange → physical activation 5. In the ring, between rounds: breathe first (4-2-6), then listen. Boxers who talk in the corner do not hear the corner / Post-bout: immediate physical recovery and medical check. No tactical analysis for 24–48 hours. Then structured video review against the Part 2 §4 KPIs, one technical fix, one tactical fix, one documented lesson.

display_text: Menstrual cycle tracking as a monitoring variable. Track alongside training load — symptoms, cycle day, and subjective performance. Individual patterns are far more useful than population generalizations. / On phase-based training periodization, be sceptical. A systematic review of menstrual cycle effects on elite athlete performance found that of 662 papers reviewed and 218 assessed for eligibility, only seven precisely investigated a performance parameter across at least one cycle phase in elite athletes — and concluded that while various parameters are affected, the parameters themselves and the magnitude and direction of effects are inconclusive (Meignié et al., 2021). A more recent review in the strength and conditioning literature stated the position plainly: research does not currently support the idea that periodizing strength or endurance training according to the menstrual cycle confers additional benefit over traditional approaches. / Practical position: track the cycle, learn *your own* patterns, adjust individually based on your data, and do not adopt a rigid phase-based template on the basis of social media claims. If you consistently perform worse or feel worse in a particular phase, that is real for you and worth accommodating.

display_text: The Amsterdam 2023 international consensus statement (Patricios et al., 2023, *BJSM* — the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport) provides the current framework, including an updated staged return-to-play protocol and updated assessment tools (SCAT6, Child SCAT6, SCOAT6, CRT6). The consensus organizes clinical management around a framework of “R”s — Recognize, Reduce, Remove, Re-evaluate, (Relative) Rest, Rehabilitate, Refer, Recover, Return-to-Learn/Return-to-Sport, Reconsider, Refine, and Retire — the last two being additions in the Amsterdam statement. / The staged progression, adapted for boxing: / | Stage | Activity | Boxing content | Criteria to progress | / | 1 | Symptom-limited activity | Daily activities that do not exacerbate symptoms; light walking | Tolerated without symptom exacerbation | / | 2 | Light aerobic exercise | Walking, stationary bike at low intensity | 24 h symptom-free at this level | / | 3 | Sport-specific exercise, no head impact | Shadow boxing, footwork, light bag work, running | 24 h symptom-free | / | 4 | Non-contact training drills | Full technical training, pads, bag work at normal intensity, conditioning, strength training | 24 h symptom-free | / | 5 | Full contact practice — requires medical clearance | Return to sparring, beginning at Stage 3–4 of the sparring continuum, not at the level you left | Medical clearance obtained; no symptoms | / | 6 | Return to competition | Normal competitive activity | All above cleared | / Rules: - Each stage requires at least 24 hours symptom-free before progressing - Any symptom recurrence returns the athlete to the previous stage - Stage 5 requires medical clearance, without exception - On return to sparring, drop back two stages of the sparring continuum and rebuild. Returning directly to hard sparring after a concussion is how second injuries happen - Most jurisdictions impose mandatory suspension periods after knockouts and technical knockouts — treat these as minimums, not targets, and extend generously

display_text: The IOC consensus emphasizes that inadvertent ingestion of prohibited substances via supplements is a documented and real risk. Any boxer subject to testing — which includes all sanctioned amateur competition and most professional commissions — must: / 1. Use only third-party batch-certified products (Informed Sport, NSF Certified for Sport, or equivalent) / 2. Retain records of every batch used — product, batch number, dates / 3. Conduct a genuine risk-benefit analysis before taking anything / 4. Understand strict liability — the athlete is responsible for what is in their body regardless of how it got there / A marginal performance gain is not worth a career-ending sanction. The IOC statement itself provides a decision flow chart for exactly this analysis.

display_text: Meta-analytic work on tapering is unusually clear and unusually actionable. Bosquet et al. (2007), pooling 27 studies of competitive athletes, found: / - Overall taper effect on performance: 0.59 (moderate) / - Optimal strategy: a 2-week taper in which training volume is reduced exponentially by 41–60% (effect 0.72), with no modification of training intensity (effect 0.33 for maintained intensity) or frequency (0.35 for maintained frequency) / - Reducing intensity does not improve performance / A more recent systematic review and meta-analysis in endurance athletes (Chen et al., 2023) confirmed the pattern: reducing volume 41–60% while maintaining intensity and frequency, over ≤7 days, 8–14 days, or 15–21 days, in either a progressive or step pattern, significantly improved time-trial performance — and a taper preceded by a pre-taper overload block produced larger gains than a conventional taper. / Note also, relevant to strength retention: reduced-volume training during a taper clearly beats stopping altogether. Complete cessation for several weeks costs roughly twice the strength and velocity that maintained lower-volume training does. / Bosquet et al. display_text: Diaphragmatic breathing — daily, 5–10 min - Sit or lie with one hand on the belly, one on the chest. The belly hand moves; the chest hand does not - Progress to a 4-2-6 pattern: inhale 4 s, hold 2 s, exhale 6 s. The extended exhale is the parasympathetic driver - Then practise it in the 60-second interval between rounds, on the bag and in sparring, until it is automatic. This is the transfer step everyone omits - Morning and pre-sleep / Progressive muscular relaxation — 2×/week, 15–20 min - Full-body protocol: tense each muscle group 5 s, release 15 s, moving systematically - Then build an abbreviated version usable in the ring: jaw, shoulders, hands — three checkpoints you can run in two seconds between exchanges / Cue words for relaxation - Anchor 2–3 words during training (“loose,” “breathe,” “long,” “soft hands”) and deploy them in competition - The anchoring matters: the word must be paired with the physical state hundreds of times in training before it will produce the state under pressure / HRV biofeedback — 3–5×/week, 10–15 min, if available - Resonance-frequency breathing training with a validated app and a chest strap - The evidence is moderate and the practice is harmless; worth doing if you will do it consistently

display_text: Suspect concussion after any blow to the head, face, neck, or body that transmits force to the head, if any of the following appear: / Symptoms: headache, pressure in the head, dizziness, nausea, blurred or double vision, sensitivity to light or noise, feeling “slowed down,” “in a fog,” “not right,” difficulty concentrating or remembering, fatigue, irritability, emotional lability, sleep disturbance. / Signs: loss of consciousness (in only a minority of concussions), blank or vacant look, lying motionless, slow to get up, unsteadiness, disorientation, confusion, inability to respond appropriately, facial injury with any of the above, seizure, tonic posturing. / Immediate red flags requiring emergency evaluation: neck pain or tenderness, double vision, weakness or tingling in limbs, severe or increasing headache, seizure, loss of consciousness, deteriorating consciousness, vomiting, increasing restlessness or agitation.
